justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assumed was a recent price level near 313–314, likely referencing an asset trading in that range—most consistent with something like the S&P 500 ETF (SPY) or a similar broad index instrument. For the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price with only a slight positive bias, reflecting the historical tendency for equity markets to have a marginally positive expected daily return while acknowledging that a single day offers almost no time for meaningful trend development. At one week, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to around 316, incorporating a small momentum or drift assumption. At one month, I moved to 318, extrapolating a gentle upward trajectory consistent with long-run equity market behavior, while recognizing that a month is long enough for meaningful macro developments to shift prices materially.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to typical realized volatility at each horizon. For a single day, historical daily moves of roughly 0.5–1% in either direction for a broad index justified a relatively tight band of about plus or minus 10–11 points. At one week, volatility scales approximately with the square root of time, widening the interval to roughly plus or minus 20 points. At one month, that scaling continues, producing a band of about plus or minus 38–40 points, reflecting the compounding of daily uncertainty over approximately 21 trading days. Implied volatility conditions and the current macro environment would normally sharpen or widen these bands further, but without real-time options data I defaulted to historically grounded estimates.

Several risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in inflation data, an unexpected hawkish pivot from the Federal Reserve, a geopolitical shock, or a significant credit event could easily drive prices below the lower bounds, particularly at the one-week and one-month horizons. Liquidity stress or a flash crash event could even breach the one-day lower bound. On the upside, a surprise dovish signal from central banks, a strong earnings season, or a resolution of geopolitical tensions could fuel a rally that exceeds my upper bounds. The one-month interval is the most vulnerable to being breached simply because more time means more opportunity for compounding surprises, and fat-tailed return distributions mean that true tail probabilities are higher than a normal distribution assumption would imply.
